title: Minimum Replacements to Sort the Array
statement:
You have a 0-indexed array `nums` of positive integers. A single operation takes one element out of the array and puts two positive integers whose sum equals that element in its place, in the same position.

Return the smallest number of operations after which the array reads in non-decreasing order from left to right.
notes:
## Intuition

The last element never needs cutting: splitting it only makes the right end smaller, which can only tighten the limit on everything before it. So walk from right to left, keeping `bound`, the value the element to the left must not exceed. An element above `bound` must be cut into at least `ceil(value / bound)` pieces, and using exactly that many pieces, as evenly as possible, leaves the biggest possible leftmost piece, which is the loosest limit for the elements still to the left. Trying every cut is exponential; this greedy choice is optimal at each step.

## Approach

1. Set `bound` to the last element and `operations` to 0.
2. Walk `i` from the second-to-last index down to 0, reading `value = nums[i]`.
3. If `value <= bound`, it fits as it is; it becomes the new `bound`.
4. Otherwise cut it into `pieces = ceil(value / bound)` parts, which costs `pieces - 1` operations.
5. Spread the parts evenly, so the smallest one, `floor(value / pieces)`, becomes the new `bound`.
6. Return `operations`.

## Example 1, step by step

`nums = [3, 9, 3]`. Start with `bound = 3`. At `i = 1`, `value = 9 > 3`, so `pieces = ceil(9 / 3) = 3`, `operations = 2` and `bound = floor(9 / 3) = 3` (the pieces are `3, 3, 3`). At `i = 0`, `value = 3 <= 3`, so nothing changes. The answer is `2`.

## Complexity

- Time: O(n): one pass with constant work per element.
- Space: O(1): only a few counters.

## Pitfalls

- The new limit is the smallest piece, `floor(value / pieces)`, not `bound` itself: `[7, 6]` keeps `bound = 6` but splitting 7 gives `3, 4`, so the next limit is 3.
- Use exactly `ceil(value / bound)` pieces; more pieces only shrink the next limit.
- The total can reach about 10^14, beyond a 32-bit integer; Java and C need a 64-bit result.

## Variables

| Name | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `operations` | operations used so far |
| `bound` | largest value allowed for the element at `i` |
| `i` | index being processed, right to left |
| `value` | `nums[i]` |
| `pieces` | how many parts `value` is cut into |

narration.2: No operations have been spent yet.
narration.3: The last element is never cut, so it sets the first limit.
narration.5: Walk from the second-to-last element back to the start.
narration.6: Read the element that has to fit under the current limit.
narration.7: Does it already fit under the limit?
narration.8: Yes: it stays whole and becomes the limit for the element to its left.
narration.11: No: cut it into the fewest pieces that are each at most bound.
narration.12: Cutting into that many pieces takes one operation fewer than the piece count.
narration.13: With the pieces as even as possible, the smallest one is the new limit.
narration.15: Every element now fits; return the total number of operations.
